questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

Each of the engineers have submitted their design notes.

options.text: Each of the engineers has submitted their design notes.
Each of the engineers have submitted their design notes.
Each of the engineers has submit their design notes.
Each of the engineer have submitted their design notes.

questions.explanationText: “Each” is singular, so it takes “has” even though the noun in the of-phrase is plural.

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

Each of the applicants are required to upload a photograph.

options.text: Each of the applicants are required to upload a photograph.
Each of the applicant are required to upload a photograph.
Each of the applicants is require to upload a photograph.
Each of the applicants is required to upload a photograph.

questions.explanationText: The singular subject “each” takes “is.”

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

Each of the sensors were checked before installation.

options.text: Each of the sensor were checked before installation.
Each of the sensors was check before installation.
Each of the sensors was checked before installation.
Each of the sensors were checked before installation.

questions.explanationText: The verb agrees with singular “each,” not plural “sensors.”

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

Each of the departments have prepared its budget.

options.text: Each of the department have prepared its budget.
Each of the departments have prepared its budget.
Each of the departments has prepared its budget.
Each of the departments has prepare its budget.

questions.explanationText: The singular subject “each” requires “has.”

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

Each of the participants receive a feedback form.

options.text: Each of the participant receive a feedback form.
Each of the participants receive a feedback form.
Each of the participants are receiving a feedback form.
Each of the participants receives a feedback form.

questions.explanationText: In the simple present, singular “each” takes “receives.”

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

Each of the machines need regular calibration.

options.text: Each of the machine need regular calibration.
Each of the machines needs regular calibration.
Each of the machines need regular calibration.
Each of the machines are needing regular calibration.

questions.explanationText: The singular subject “each” requires the singular verb “needs.”

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

Each of the proposals were evaluated independently.

options.text: Each of the proposal were evaluated independently.
Each of the proposals was evaluated independently.
Each of the proposals were evaluated independently.
Each of the proposals was evaluate independently.

questions.explanationText: The passive verb must agree with singular “each.”

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

Each of the students have access to the portal.

options.text: Each of the students has access to the portal.
Each of the students have access to the portal.
Each of the student have access to the portal.
Each of the students are having access to the portal.

questions.explanationText: The head subject “each” is singular and takes “has.”

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

Each of the reports contain a summary.

options.text: Each of the reports contains a summary.
Each of the reports are containing a summary.
Each of the report contain a summary.
Each of the reports contain a summary.

questions.explanationText: The singular subject “each” requires “contains.”

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

Each of the employees are expected to attend the briefing.

options.text: Each of the employee are expected to attend the briefing.
Each of the employees are expected to attend the briefing.
Each of the employees is expected to attend the briefing.
Each of the employees is expect to attend the briefing.

questions.explanationText: The passive construction agrees with singular “each,” so “is expected” is required.

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

A number of candidates is waiting outside.

options.text: The number of candidates are waiting outside.
A number of candidate are waiting outside.
A number of candidates are waiting outside.
A number of candidates is waiting outside.

questions.explanationText: “A number of” means several and takes a plural verb.

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

The number of support requests have increased.

options.text: The number of support requests has increased.
The number of support requests have increased.
The number of support requests are increased.
A number of support requests has increased.

questions.explanationText: The head subject is the singular noun “number.”

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

One of the servers have failed.

options.text: One of the server has failed.
One of the servers are failed.
One of the servers have failed.
One of the servers has failed.

questions.explanationText: “One” is the singular subject.

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

Mathematics are essential for this role.

options.text: Mathematics were essential for this role.
Mathematics are essential for this role.
Mathematics is essential for this role.
The mathematics are essential for this role.

questions.explanationText: The name of the academic subject is grammatically singular.

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

The news about the merger are surprising.

options.text: The news of the merger are a surprise.
The news about the merger are surprising.
The news about the merger is surprising.
The news about the merger have surprised.

questions.explanationText: “News” is singular in standard English.

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

The team of analysts have completed its review.

options.text: The team of analysts have completed their review.
The team of analyst has completed its review.
The team of analysts has completed its review.
The team of analysts have completed its review.

questions.explanationText: Here “team” is treated as one unit and agrees with singular “its.”

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

Ten kilometres are a long distance to walk in this heat.

options.text: Ten kilometres are a long distance to walk in this heat.
Ten kilometres is a long distance to walk in this heat.
Ten kilometres have been a long distance to walk in this heat.
Ten kilometre is a long distance to walk in this heat.

questions.explanationText: A measurement viewed as one amount takes a singular verb.

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

The quality of the components have improved.

options.text: The quality of the components has improved.
The qualities of the components has improved.
The quality of the components have improved.
The quality of the component have improved.

questions.explanationText: The head subject “quality” is singular.

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

There is several reasons to revise the schedule.

options.text: There are several reasons to revise the schedule.
There is several reasons to revise the schedule.
There are several reason to revise the schedule.
There have several reasons to revise the schedule.

questions.explanationText: In this construction, the verb agrees with the plural noun “reasons.”

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

More than one employee have raised the issue.

options.text: More than one employee are raising the issue.
More than one employees have raised the issue.
More than one employee has raised the issue.
More than one employee have raised the issue.

questions.explanationText: “More than one” normally takes a singular noun and singular verb.

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

Neither the manager nor the employees is available.

options.text: Neither the manager or the employees are available.
Neither the manager nor the employees is available.
Neither the manager nor the employees has available.
Neither the manager nor the employees are available.

questions.explanationText: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer plural subject “employees.”

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

Neither the engineers nor the supervisor are responsible.

options.text: Neither the engineers nor the supervisor have responsibility.
Neither the engineers nor the supervisor is responsible.
Neither the engineers or the supervisor is responsible.
Neither the engineers nor the supervisor are responsible.

questions.explanationText: The nearer subject “supervisor” is singular.

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

Either the printer or the scanners needs replacement.

options.text: Either the printer nor the scanners need replacement.
Either the printer or the scanners needs replacing them.
Either the printer or the scanners needs replacement.
Either the printer or the scanners need replacement.

questions.explanationText: The verb agrees with the nearer plural subject “scanners.”

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

The report, along with its appendices, are complete.

options.text: The report, along with its appendices, are complete.
The report along its appendices are complete.
The report, along with its appendices, is complete.
The report, along with its appendices, have completed.

questions.explanationText: The phrase set off by commas does not change the singular subject “report.”

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

The director, as well as the advisers, have approved the plan.

options.text: The director, as well as the advisers, have approved the plan.
The director, as well as the advisers, has approved the plan.
The director as well the advisers has approved the plan.
The director, as well as the advisers, are approving the plan.

questions.explanationText: “As well as” does not create a compound subject here.

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

The laptop together with its accessories were delivered.

options.text: The laptop together with its accessories were delivered.
The laptop together its accessories was delivered.
The laptop, together with its accessories, have been delivered.
The laptop, together with its accessories, was delivered.

questions.explanationText: The singular head noun “laptop” controls agreement.

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

Not only the interns but also the manager were present.

options.text: Not only the interns but the manager were present.
Not only the interns and also the manager was present.
Not only the interns but also the manager were present.
Not only the interns but also the manager was present.

questions.explanationText: With not only...but also, agreement follows the nearer subject “manager.”

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

Both the router and the modem is working.

options.text: Both the router and the modem is working.
Both the router and the modem are working.
Both the router or the modem are working.
Both router and modem is working.

questions.explanationText: Two subjects joined by “and” take a plural verb.

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

Every desk and chair were inspected.

options.text: Every desk or chair were inspected.
Every desk and chair was inspected.
Every desks and chairs were inspected.
Every desk and chair were inspected.

questions.explanationText: Repeated singular items under “every” take a singular verb.

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

Either of these alternatives are acceptable.

options.text: Either these alternatives are acceptable.
Either of these alternatives is acceptable.
Either of these alternatives are acceptable.
Either of this alternatives is acceptable.

questions.explanationText: The pronoun “either” is singular.

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

She is working here since 2021.

options.text: She has been working here since 2021.
She has working here since 2021.
She was working here since 2021.
She is working here since 2021.

questions.explanationText: An action continuing from a starting point uses the present perfect continuous with “since.”

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

They have waited for the results since three hours.

options.text: They have been waiting for the results for three hours.
They have been waited for the results for three hours.
They have waited for the results since three hours.
They are waiting for the results since three hours.

questions.explanationText: Use “for” with a duration and the present perfect continuous for an ongoing action.

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

The server is offline for two hours.

options.text: The server has been offline for two hours.
The server is offline for two hours.
The server has being offline for two hours.
The server was offline since two hours.

questions.explanationText: A state continuing to the present uses the present perfect.

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

I did not receive the confirmation yet.

options.text: I have not received the confirmation yet.
I did not receive the confirmation yet.
I have not receive the confirmation yet.
I was not received the confirmation yet.

questions.explanationText: “Yet” commonly accompanies the present perfect for an unfinished present-time result.

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

The team already completed the audit.

options.text: The team had already complete the audit.
The team has already completed the audit.
The team is already completing the audit.
The team already completed the audit.

questions.explanationText: The present perfect naturally expresses a completed action with current relevance.

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

We know each other for ten years.

options.text: We know each other for ten years.
We are knowing each other for ten years.
We had knew each other for ten years.
We have known each other for ten years.

questions.explanationText: The stative verb “know” uses the present perfect, not a continuous form, for a continuing relationship.

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

He has joined the company last Monday.

options.text: He joined the company last Monday.
He had joined the company last Monday.
He has joined the company last Monday.
He has been joining the company last Monday.

questions.explanationText: A finished past time requires the simple past.

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

The researchers are collecting data since June.

options.text: The researchers were collecting data since June.
The researchers have been collecting data since June.
The researchers are collecting data since June.
The researchers have collected data since June ago.

questions.explanationText: The action began in June and continues, so present perfect continuous is appropriate.

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

This is the first time I saw this error.

options.text: This was the first time I have saw this error.
This is the first time I have seen this error.
This is the first time I am seeing this error yesterday.
This is the first time I saw this error.

questions.explanationText: After “This is the first time,” standard usage takes the present perfect.

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

The company did not announce the date so far.

options.text: The company did not announce the date so far.
The company had not announce the date so far.
The company is not announcing the date so far.
The company has not announced the date so far.

questions.explanationText: “So far” links the period to the present and calls for the present perfect.

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

By the time the meeting started, the manager already left.

options.text: By the time the meeting started, the manager already left.
By the time the meeting started, the manager had already left.
By the time the meeting starts, the manager had already left.
By the time the meeting had started, the manager already leaves.

questions.explanationText: The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect.

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

After the engineer had checked the circuit, she switches on the power.

options.text: After the engineer had checked the circuit, she switches on the power.
After the engineer has checked the circuit, she switched on the power.
After the engineer checked the circuit, she had switched on the power.
After the engineer had checked the circuit, she switched on the power.

questions.explanationText: The main past action must be in the simple past; the earlier check is past perfect.

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

When we reached the station, the train has departed.

options.text: When we had reached the station, the train departs.
When we reach the station, the train had departed.
When we reached the station, the train has departed.
When we reached the station, the train had departed.

questions.explanationText: Departure occurred before the later past arrival.

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

The analyst realised that she entered the wrong value.

options.text: The analyst realised that she entered the wrong value.
The analyst had realised that she enters the wrong value.
The analyst realised that she had entered the wrong value.
The analyst realises that she had entered the wrong value yesterday.

questions.explanationText: The entry preceded the past realisation, so past perfect clarifies the sequence.

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

No sooner had the alarm sounded when the staff evacuated.

options.text: No sooner the alarm had sounded than the staff evacuated.
No sooner had the alarm sounded than the staff evacuated.
No sooner had the alarm sound than the staff evacuated.
No sooner had the alarm sounded when the staff evacuated.

questions.explanationText: The standard correlative construction is “no sooner...than.”

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

Hardly had the test begun than the power failed.

options.text: Hardly had the test begun when the power failed.
Hardly the test had begun when the power failed.
Hardly had the test began when the power failed.
Hardly had the test begun than the power failed.

questions.explanationText: “Hardly” pairs with “when,” and “begun” is the correct participle.

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

Before the patch was released, the team tests it thoroughly.

options.text: Before the patch was released, the team has tested it thoroughly.
Before the patch had released, the team tested it thoroughly.
Before the patch was released, the team tests it thoroughly.
Before the patch was released, the team had tested it thoroughly.

questions.explanationText: The testing was completed before another past event.

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

The road was flooded because it rained heavily all night.

options.text: The road was flooded because it had rained heavily all night.
The road was flooded because it rained heavily all night.
The road was flooding because it has rained all night.
The road had flooded because it was raining tomorrow.

questions.explanationText: Past perfect appropriately marks the prior cause of the past condition.

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

She submitted the form after she verifies every entry.

options.text: She had submitted the form after she verifies every entry.
She submits the form after she had verified every entry.
She submitted the form after she had verified every entry.
She submitted the form after she verifies every entry.

questions.explanationText: Verification was completed before the past submission.

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

The device stopped because the battery was not charged.

options.text: The device stops because the battery had not charge.
The device stopped because the battery was not charged.
The device stopped because the battery had not been charged.
The device had stopped because the battery is not charged.

questions.explanationText: The lack of charging preceded the device’s past stoppage.

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

When the vendor will arrive, we will inspect the goods.

options.text: When the vendor will arrive, we will inspect the goods.
When the vendor arrived, we will inspect the goods.
When the vendor will arrives, we inspect the goods.
When the vendor arrives, we will inspect the goods.

questions.explanationText: A future time clause uses the simple present, not “will.”

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

We will begin the test after the supervisor will approve the setup.

options.text: We will began the test after the supervisor approves the setup.
We begin the test after the supervisor will approve the setup.
We will begin the test after the supervisor will approve the setup.
We will begin the test after the supervisor approves the setup.

questions.explanationText: Use simple present in the future time clause after “after.”

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

As soon as the data will be available, the model will be retrained.

options.text: As soon as the data will be available, the model will be retrained.
As soon as the data are available, the model will be retrained.
As soon as the data were available, the model will retrain.
As soon as the data will available, the model is retrained.

questions.explanationText: The as-soon-as clause takes present tense for future reference.

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

Before you will submit the form, check the account number.

options.text: Before you submit the form, check the account number.
Before you will submits the form, checking the account number.
Before you will submit the form, check the account number.
Before you submitted the form, check the account number.

questions.explanationText: The time clause uses simple present.

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

Until the issue will be resolved, the service will remain offline.

options.text: Until the issue is resolved, the service will remain offline.
Until the issue will resolve, the service remains offline.
Until the issue was resolved, the service will remain offline.
Until the issue will be resolved, the service will remain offline.

questions.explanationText: “Until” introduces a present-tense clause with future meaning.

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

Once the committee will decide, we will publish the result.

options.text: Once the committee decides, we will publish the result.
Once the committee will decide, we will publish the result.
Once the committee decided, we will publish the result.
Once the committee will decides, we publish the result.

questions.explanationText: Use simple present after “once” for a future condition.

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

I will call you when I will reach the office.

options.text: I will call you when I will reach the office.
I call you when I will reach the office.
I will called you when I reach the office.
I will call you when I reach the office.

questions.explanationText: The main clause takes “will”; the when-clause takes simple present.

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

The machine will restart after the temperature will fall.

options.text: The machine will restart after the temperature falls.
The machine will restart after the temperature will fall.
The machine restarts after the temperature will fall.
The machine will restarting after the temperature falls.

questions.explanationText: Future time clauses do not normally use “will.”

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

By the time you will return, we will have finished the review.

options.text: By the time you will return, we have finished the review.
By the time you return, we will have finished the review.
By the time you returned, we will finish the review.
By the time you will return, we will have finished the review.

questions.explanationText: The time clause uses present simple; the main clause correctly uses future perfect.

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

Unless the client will object, the change will take effect tomorrow.

options.text: Unless the client objects, the change will take effect tomorrow.
Unless the client will objects, the change takes effect tomorrow.
Unless the client objected, the change will take effect tomorrow.
Unless the client will object, the change will take effect tomorrow.

questions.explanationText: In a real future condition, the unless-clause uses simple present.

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

Me and Rina prepared the presentation.

options.text: Rina and me prepared the presentation.
Rina and I prepared the presentation.
Me and Rina prepared the presentation.
I and Rina has prepared the presentation.

questions.explanationText: A subject position requires “I,” and conventional order places the other person first.

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

The manager spoke to Ravi and I.

options.text: The manager spoke to Ravi and me.
The manager spoke to Ravi and myself.
The manager spoke with Ravi and I.
The manager spoke to Ravi and I.

questions.explanationText: The object of the preposition “to” requires the objective form “me.”

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

Between you and I, the estimate is too low.

options.text: Between you and me, the estimate is too low.
Between yourself and I, the estimate is too low.
Among you and me, the estimate is too low.
Between you and I, the estimate is too low.

questions.explanationText: “Between” is followed by object pronouns.

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

The award was given to she.

options.text: The award was given to her.
The award was given to she.
The award was given to herself.
The award was gave to her.

questions.explanationText: The preposition “to” requires the object pronoun “her.”

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

Him and his colleague joined the call.

options.text: His colleague and him joined the call.
He and his colleague joined the call.
Him and his colleague joined the call.
He and his colleague joins the call.

questions.explanationText: The compound subject requires the subject pronoun “he.”

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

The director invited my colleague and myself.

options.text: The director invited my colleague and I.
The director invited I and my colleague.
The director invited my colleague and me.
The director invited my colleague and myself.

questions.explanationText: A reflexive pronoun is inappropriate without a co-referential subject; use “me.”

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

Who did the panel select for the role?

options.text: Whose did the panel select for the role?
Whom did the panel select for the role?
Who did the panel select for the role?
Whom did the panel selected for the role?

questions.explanationText: Formal usage requires “whom” as the object of “select.”

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

Whom is leading the investigation?

options.text: Who are leading the investigation?
Who is leading the investigation?
Whom is leading the investigation?
Whom does lead the investigation?

questions.explanationText: The questioned word is the subject, so “who” is required.

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

The final decision rests with he and the chairperson.

options.text: The final decision rest with him and the chairperson.
The final decision rests with himself and the chairperson.
The final decision rests with he and the chairperson.
The final decision rests with him and the chairperson.

questions.explanationText: The object of “with” must be “him.”

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

Us engineers must verify the drawing.

options.text: Our engineers must to verify the drawing.
We engineers must verifies the drawing.
We engineers must verify the drawing.
Us engineers must verify the drawing.

questions.explanationText: The appositive phrase functions as the subject, so “we” is correct.

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

Every candidate must bring their own identity card.

options.text: Every candidate must bring their own identity card.
Every candidate must bring they own identity card.
Every candidate must brings their own identity card.
Every candidates must bring their own identity card.

questions.explanationText: Singular “they/their” is standard and avoids unnecessary gender marking; the original is correct.

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

The company changed it’s policy.

options.text: The company changed it’s policy.
The company changed their policy itself.
The company changed its policy.
The company change its policy.

questions.explanationText: “Its” is possessive; “it’s” means “it is” or “it has.”

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

The engineers blamed theirselves for the delay.

options.text: The engineers blamed themselves for the delay.
The engineers blamed theirselves about the delay.
The engineers blamed theirselves for the delay.
The engineers blamed themself for the delay.

questions.explanationText: The correct plural reflexive pronoun is “themselves.”

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

She herself completed the audit.

options.text: She herself completed the audit.
She completed herself the audit.
Her herself completed the audit.
She herself have completed the audit.

questions.explanationText: The emphatic reflexive correctly refers back to “she”; no correction is needed.

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

When Maya spoke to Leena, she was upset.

options.text: When Maya spoke to Leena, she was upset.
When Maya spoke to Leena, they was upset.
Speaking to Leena, she upset Maya.
Maya was upset when she spoke to Leena.

questions.explanationText: Naming Maya as the upset person removes the ambiguous reference.

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

The laptop was placed beside the tablet, but it was damaged.

options.text: The damaged laptop was placed beside the tablet.
The laptop was placed beside the damaged tablet, but it was damaged.
The laptop beside the tablet damaged it.
The laptop was placed beside the tablet, but it was damaged.

questions.explanationText: The revision explicitly identifies the laptop as damaged and removes the ambiguous “it.”

questions.questionText:
Select the best correction without changing the intended meaning.

One should keep your password confidential.

options.text: One should keep your password confidential.
One should keep one’s password confidential.
One should keeps their password confidential.
One should keep you password confidential.

questions.explanationText: Formal consistency requires “one...one’s.”

questions.questionText:
Which option provides the best sentence improvement?

The team completed its task by themselves.

options.text: The team completed its task by itself.
The team completed their task by itself.
The team completed its task by themselves.
The team complete its task by themselves.

questions.explanationText: Singular “team” and “its” call for the singular reflexive “itself.”

questions.questionText:
Identify the sentence that is grammatically and logically correct.

Please contact either Rohan or myself.

options.text: Please contact either Rohan or myself.
Please contact either Rohan or me.
Please contact either Rohan or yourself.
Please contact either Rohan or I.

questions.explanationText: “Me” is the object of “contact”; “myself” lacks a matching subject antecedent.

questions.questionText:
Choose the most appropriate revision.

This is the engineer which designed the sensor.

options.text: This is the engineer which designed the sensor.
This is the engineer whom designed the sensor.
This is the engineer who designed the sensor.
This is the engineer whose designed the sensor.

questions.explanationText: Use “who” for a person functioning as the subject of the relative clause.

questions.questionText:
Choose the grammatically correct version.

She is an university researcher.

options.text: She is an university researcher.
